Estimate PSFs

Source: vignettes/articles/estimate-psf.Rmd
estimate-psf.Rmd

A short impulse is often recorded as a wider response: an optical blur, an instrument response or a chromatographic peak. Its point spread function (PSF) describes that response. With a known time-invariant PSF, shifted copies form a convolution design matrix, and l0glmFit() can estimate a sparse set of impulse locations and amplitudes directly.

When the PSF is unknown, alternate two conditional fits. Estimate the spike train with the current kernel, then estimate the kernel with those spikes held fixed. estimatePSF() can also calibrate the kernel from isolated standards and estimate how it changes across overlapping windows.

The resulting sparse matrix X serves two purposes. Use it directly in l0glmFit() when a common response shape at each position is adequate. Use it to initialize log-concave NMF when components at the same position may have different widths or tails.

Deconvolve with a known, constant PSF

This multichannel signal has eight impulses, an asymmetric bigaussian PSF with left and right widths of 1.25 and 5 scans, and Poisson noise. Channels share impulse locations but have different amplitudes.

library(L0glm)
library(logconNMF)
set.seed(611)
n <- 600L; m <- 6L
time <- seq_len(n) / 50
g <- convKernel("bigaussian", 51L, list(sigma1=1.25, sigma2=5),
  perc="mean")
X <- convMatrix(g, n)
A <- matrix(0, n, m)
A[c(65,125,190,255,335,405,475,540),] <- runif(8L*m, 1500, 3500)
Y <- matrix(rpois(n*m, as.matrix(X %*% A)+3), n, m)

known <- l0glmFit(X, Y, family=poisson("identity"), offset=3,
  nonnegative=TRUE, grouped=TRUE, relaxed=TRUE)

Selected rows in coef(known) locate the impulses. The fixed-PSF tutorial develops this regression model.

Estimate an unknown kernel from overlapping signals 

initial <- convKernel("gaussian", 51L, list(sigma=4))
blind <- estimatePSF(Y, time=time, family=poisson("identity"),
  standard=NULL, method="blind", nwindows=1L, precluster=1L,
  offset=3, control=list(kernel_est=initial, maxiter=6L))
blind$g_hat
blind$width_scans

nwindows=1L estimates one common PSF. The symmetric Gaussian start is refined into an asymmetric response. The estimator starts with a positive normalized kernel, alternates spike and kernel fits, and retains the completed fit with the best requested information criterion. Unit-sum normalization places scale in spike amplitudes; centroid alignment fixes the shift convention.

The default precluster=1L uses the total across channels. FALSE uses the original channels; an integer requests at most that many intensity-adjusted groups. The returned blind$X is a sparse scan-by-scan design ready for l0glmFit() or logconNMF().

Calibrate from isolated standard peaks 

standard_spikes <- numeric(n)
standard_spikes[c(90,300,510)] <- c(12000,18000,15000)
standard <- list(Y=rpois(n, as.numeric(X %*% standard_spikes)+5), time=time)

calibrated <- estimatePSF(Y, time=time, standard=standard,
  family=poisson("identity"), method="standard", nwindows=1L,
  control=list(L=51L, baseline_df=4L, n_peaks=3L))

Calibration estimates a low-quantile background, identifies informative isolated peaks and fits their log-concave profiles using the observation likelihood. Normalized profiles are aligned by centroid and placed on the sample scan interval. method="standard" retains this calibration; method="auto" uses it to initialize blind refinement on the sample.

Asymmetric bigaussian ground truth, symmetric initialization, blind and calibrated PSFs, and window-specific estimates

Allow the PSF to vary through the signal 

varying <- estimatePSF(Y, time=time, standard=standard,
  family=poisson("identity"), method="auto", nwindows=3L,
  offset=3, control=list(L=51L, baseline_df=4L, n_peaks=3L, maxiter=6L))
varying$psf_timepoints
varying$psf_kernels
dim(varying$X)

Local kernels are estimated in overlapping windows and joined smoothly on their log-profile scale. Each column of varying$X represents the response appropriate to that impulse position. This synthetic signal has a constant true kernel, so its local estimates should be similar; the same construction captures gradual changes in instrumental response.

For an experimental example, bundled matrices include an alkane calibration signal in alkanes_TIC, whose named time coordinate is recognized automatically:

data(gcmsData2)
psf <- estimatePSF(gcmsData2, nwindows=3L, method="standard")
psf$method
psf$aggregation

Reuse one standard across samples

Fit the total-ion chromatogram of an isolated-peak standard once, after excluding the solvent region. Pass times explicitly for an unnamed vector. Then use its calibration to build a sparse convolution design on each sample’s scan grid:

keep <- standard_time >= 3  # minutes; choose the end of the solvent interval
calibration <- estimatePSF(standard_tic[keep], time=standard_time[keep],
  method="standard", nwindows=10L)
psf <- estimatePSF(sample_signal, time=sample_time, standard=calibration,
  method="standard", nwindows=10L)
X <- psf$X

The standard’s local peak shapes are reused. Each sample gets a design on its own time grid and can have a different number of scans. Use method="auto" if the sample also needs blind refinement from those starting shapes.

Gaussian, Poisson, quasipoisson, NB2, NB1 and the two Gamma parameterizations are supported with identity links. Noise scales are shared across channels. Aggregation diagnostics record the variance matching used in reduced models.

A position-dependent PSF describes a common instrumental response. Components whose shapes also depend on their identity or intensity can be modeled using sparse log-concave NMF. The mathematical article gives the objectives, initialization and pseudocode. File-based calibration and automated reports are available in GCMSprime.
